title_original: Sophie Calle, Between Art and Life

blocks.text: Born in Paris in 1953, Sophie Calle has spent nearly half a century turning her own life, and the lives of strangers, into material for art. Back in Paris in the late 1970s after years of travel, she began following people in the street, then invited strangers to sleep in her bed for “Les Dormeurs” (1979) and trailed a man all the way to Venice for “Suite vénitienne” (1980). In 1981, she took a job as a chambermaid in a Venetian hotel to photograph the belongings of its guests for “L’Hôtel.” Combining photographs and texts, her projects explore surveillance, intimacy, absence and loss, from “Les Aveugles” (1986), in which people born blind described their image of beauty, to “Prenez soin de vous,” shown in the French Pavilion at the 2007 Venice Biennale. She received the Hasselblad Award in 2010.

This segment comes from “Between Worlds,” an episode of the twelfth season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in October 2025. It follows Calle from the Musée Picasso in Paris, where she staged “À toi de faire, ma mignonne” in 2023, to the cryptoporticus of Arles, the ancient Roman galleries beneath the town hall where, for the 2024 Rencontres d’Arles, she left photographs from “Les Aveugles,” already damaged by humidity, to finish decaying.
